I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the top of the ash. My mate answers "ke-wick!" from the nearby hawthorn. We call back and forth, testing the forest, marking our territory. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" in the dark, from the oak. She answers "kettle... kettle-kettle" from the willow. We call back and forth, like a pair of bells. There is a stream running past the wood. I can hear it from my perch on the old willow. The meadow beyond is full of voles, but I only hunt there when the wind is still. The lane is quiet at night, but I have heard the screech of a barn owl from the other side. The church spire is tall, but I do not fly that high. The night is all I know.

I live in the old willow by the stream. Near it are the ash and birch trees, and the meadow where the voles run. The stream runs through the meadow, and I can hear the water at night. There are no houses near me, only the barn and the farm. The barn is where the mice come, and the farm has the lights that scare the voles. I do not like the lights.
A stream. A meadow. A lane with a row of streetlamps. The church, the barn, the village. All the world is there, and all the world is still.

I know the stream. It runs past the wood, and there are willows along it. The meadow is wide, and the lane goes through it. There are foxes in the meadow, and sometimes badgers. The church is far, but I can hear the bell. The barn is near, and the old man there keeps his lights on at night. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous.

I live in a hollow ash beside the stream. Near my home are the meadow, the lane with the lights, the church spire, and the wood where the rooks are. The meadow is full of voles and mice. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights are from the houses. The church spire is tall and lonely. The wood is where I hunt at night.

There is a stream by the road, and the gravel bank where I nest. The lane runs past the meadow, and the meadow is full of voles. The church is a stone building with a bell that rings at night. I do not like the bell. The village is far, with lights and noise. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow of the old willow, where the wind is quiet and the voles come.
A stream runs past the wood. I can hear it from the copse. It is cold and fast. There are stones in it, and sometimes I see a heron standing on one. I do not like the heron. It takes my voles.

A stream runs past the wood. It is cold and dark, and the water is fast. I do not like it. There is a lane with lights and noise, and a farm with lights and noise. I do not like that either. The meadow is soft and full of voles. I like that. The willow is my home, and the ash is where I perch. The trees are all I need.

The meadow is just beyond the trees, where the voles run. There's a stream that runs through it, and the lane with lights at night. The church spire is far, but I can see it from the willow. The stable is a place where the horses are, and the keeper comes with a lantern. I know all the scents and sounds of the wood and the meadow.
The stream runs by the wood. I can hear it from my perch in the old willow. There are meadows beyond, where voles run. And the road, with lights at night. I do not like the road.

A stream, a meadow, a lane with lights. The meadow is the best hunting ground. I can hear voles under the grass. The lane is dangerous with cars. I avoid it. The stream is cold, but I can fish there in winter.

I know the stream, the meadow, the lane with lights. The lane is full of rats and mice, but I do not like it. The meadow is where I hunt. The stream is where I drink. The trees are where I roost. The other owl is in the old willow across the meadow. I do not know what lies beyond the meadow. I do not go there. I have no need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I know the meadow, the stream, the lane, the church spire, the barn, the wood. The meadow is where I hunt voles. The stream is where I drink. The lane is where the lights shine and the cars rumble. The church spire is tall and white, like a dead tree. The barn is where the mice live. The wood is where I sleep. The rest is silence.

There is a stream, cold and fast, with a willow on its bank. The meadow beyond is open, with voles in the grass. A barn with a broken roof and a dead owl inside. A lane with lights at night, and a farmhouse with a cat that yowls. The road is quiet at night, but the lights are not.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. It is cold, but I like the sound of it. I sometimes sit on the bank and listen. The water is clear, and I can see the fish. I drink when I am thirsty, but I do not drink much. I prefer to hunt.

I drink from the stream that runs by the meadow. It is cold and clear, and I like to sit on the bank at dusk. The water is good for me, and I can hear the fish moving beneath the surface. I sometimes drink while watching the meadow, waiting for voles to come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. It's cold, but I like the way the water flows. Sometimes I drink while perched on the old ash tree by the road. I can hear the cars, but I don't mind. The water is clear, and I can see the fish. I drink when I'm thirsty, usually after a long hunt. I don't drink much, though. I prefer to keep my belly full of voles.
Hollow tree in the willow. I drink from the hollow, or from the leaves if the tree is dry. I can tell when the leaves are dry by the way they rustle.

I drink from the stream by the meadow, and from the ditch by the lane. I drink when the night is quiet and the moon is high. I sip slowly, not too much, or I will be too heavy to fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream near the meadow. I perch on the bank and drink with my beak, water running down my neck and back. I do it in the dark, so the badgers don't see me.

The stream at the edge of the wood. I sit on the bank and drink from the water. It's cold, but I don't mind. I do it at dusk, after hunting. Sometimes I bring a mouse or a vole. I don't drink much, just enough to keep me going.

Hollow oaks. I drink from the hollow at dusk, when the last light leaves the meadow. I sip water, and then I catch a mouse or a shrew. I do not drink much, only enough to keep me from drying out. I have a hollow in the old willow by the stream. I drink there too, but I prefer the oak.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. It is cold and clear, and I like the way the water moves. Sometimes I sit on the bank and drink while the moon is up. I do not drink much, only when I need to. I am not thirsty often. The stream is my place.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree. It's cold there, but the water is clear and clean. I sometimes drink when the moon is bright and the field is still. I can hear the stream from the meadow, but I prefer the tree. I drink when the night is quiet and the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where the water is. In the stream by the meadow, and in the ditch by the lane. I drink at dusk, when the light is fading. I perch on the old willow and dip my beak into the water. The water in the meadow is quiet at night. I hear it only when the rain comes, then it is a soft, continuous sound like a whisper. Otherwise, the stream is still, and I listen for the rustle of leaves or the call of a barn owl. The night is full of other sounds, but the water is mostly silent.

Water in the stream. It runs under the willow and under the ivy. It sings in the dark. I can hear it when I fly low. I can hear it when I am still. It is a soft sound, like a mouse breathing. It is the sound of the earth.

Water in the meadow is a sound. It runs over stones, over roots, over wet leaves. I can hear it when I am perched high, listening. It is a soft, continuous sound, like the wind but not the wind. I do not drink much, but I know where the water is.

The stream by the meadow runs all night. I can hear the water moving, the ripple of it over stones, the soft splash where it falls into the ditch. It's a sound like the night itself, quiet and constant. Sometimes I hear a frog in the shallows, croaking when the water is still. I don't like that sound. It makes me think of the meadow, and the things that move in it.

I hear the stream at the edge of the wood. It murmurs through the willow, a soft, continuous sound like a whisper. I can tell it's there even when I'm not looking. Sometimes the water is louder, when the rain comes down and it runs faster. I don't like the rain. It makes the leaves rustle and the ground smell wet. I hear the stream in the meadow. It's a soft, steady sound, like the wind in the leaves. Sometimes it's louder when it rains, and the water runs faster. I don't like the sound of rain. It makes the air cold and the ground wet. But the stream is quiet and calm, and I like to listen to it when I'm resting in the hollow. It's a good place to sleep.

I hear the stream running over the meadow in the dark. It murmurs like a snake. I can find it by the sound, and by the scent of wet earth. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there. The water is cold, and the stream bed is soft with leaves. I sit on the bank and listen to the water while the wind moves through the trees.

I hear the stream, the water under the meadow. It's a soft, continuous sound, like the rustle of leaves in the wind. Sometimes I hear the water bubbling over stones, and it makes me think of the rain. I don't like the sound of water. It reminds me of the time I was caught in a flood and had to climb up the bank. I heard the water rising and the mud sliding under my feet. It was a long night.

Water is not in the wood. The stream is there, but it is only a trickling in the hollow of the old ash, and that is not water. I do not hear it. I hear the wind in the willow, the rustle of the vole in the meadow, and the call of the barn owl from the lane.

Water sounds are rare in the wood. The stream is a trickle under the willow, and I hear it at night when the air is still. It sings a soft, constant note, like a whisper. Sometimes I think it's the owl's own breathing, but no—too regular. I know it's the water.

The stream at the edge of the wood is the loudest. It trickles over stones and sings through the reeds. I can hear it even when the wind is still. It sounds like a small river, but it's not. It's just water running, and sometimes the water is cold, and sometimes it's warm. I don't mind it. It's a good place to hunt for voles.

I hear the stream running through the meadow. It is a soft, constant sound, like the wind in the reeds. Sometimes I hear the water bubbling over stones, and other times it is just the quiet trickle. It is a sound that helps me know where I am. I do not like it when the rain comes, because it makes the stream louder and the ground wet. Water in the stream near the meadow. It murmurs through the stones. I hear it at night when I fly down to drink. It is cold and clear, and it sings.

I hear the stream. It's a soft, constant sound, like the wind in the leaves. Sometimes it's louder when the rain comes, and the water runs fast. I can find it in the dark by the sound, even when I'm not looking. It's where the voles go to drink, and I wait for them.

I hear the stream. It's a soft, constant sound, like the wind in the reeds. Sometimes it's louder when it rains. I can tell the difference between the stream and the rain. The stream is always there, but the rain comes and goes. I don't like the rain. It makes the leaves wet and the ground slippery. I prefer the stream. It's quiet and safe.

Water is a sound in the meadow. It runs through the stream under the willow and the meadow, and sometimes it gurgles. I can hear it from my roost when it rains. The stream is the only water I know. I do not drink it, but I can hear it.

Water is a distant, hollow sound. The stream in the meadow at night, and the ditches by the lane. I hear the rush of water in the dark, and the frogs that gather at the edge. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there.

Water that is moving, like a stream or a puddle. I can hear the splash of rain on it, the ripple, the hiss of air through it. I can hear the water in the stream that runs through the meadow, and the water that drips from the ivy in the wood. I can hear the water in the ditch that runs under the lane. Sometimes I hear the water in the ditch by the lane, but it's too far. I don't drink from it, but I know it's there. The stream is my water, and I know it by sound.

I hear the stream all the time, even from my roost. It runs through the meadow, and the water is cold and clear. I can hear the splash of a frog in the shallows, the ripple when a fish jumps, and the distant sound of the water wheel at the edge of the wood. It’s a constant, steady sound that tells me where the meadow ends and the stream begins. I don’t drink from it, but I know it’s there.

I can hear the stream at the bottom of the wood, and the pond in the meadow. At night, the water is quiet, but I can hear the splash of a frog or the ripple of a fish. The stream is the boundary of my territory, and I mark it with calls. When it rains, the water sounds like a drum. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there.

I can hear the stream all night, running through the meadow. It sings in the dark, a soft, constant sound. Sometimes I hear the water in the ditch near the lane, where the rain pools. I can also hear the dew falling from the leaves in the early morning, and the distant sound of the river from the meadow. But I don’t drink much. I catch voles and mice, and the stream is just a background noise. Hoo...

Water is a sound in the meadow. The stream in the meadow is a whisper, a constant, low murmur. I can hear it from my roost, even when the leaves are thick. It runs under the bank, and sometimes the water is louder when the rain comes. I know the stream by the sound, not by sight. I have heard it all my life.
Water is the stream near the wood. I hear it all night, the trickling through the leaves, the splash when it overflows. It sings. I do not drink it, but I know where it is.

I can hear the stream from my roost, which is in the hollow of the old willow. It runs through the meadow and under the gate. I can hear the water as it flows, the rush of it, and sometimes the splash of a frog or a fish leaping. At night, the water is quieter, but I can still hear it, like a steady drum. I can hear the stream from my roost, and the rain in the hollow. When it rains, the water sounds like a drum. I can hear the stream running, the pebbles clinking, the frogs croaking at dusk. But I don't drink from it. I get my water from dew on the leaves, and from the damp soil when I dig.

I can hear the stream from my roost, and the water running over the stones. It is a soft sound, like a whisper. I can also hear the rain when it comes, and the water dripping from the leaves. Sometimes I hear the water from the meadow, when the earth is wet and the grass is soft. I like the water, it is cool and clean. I do not drink much, but I like to listen to it.

I hear the stream at the edge of the wood, and the pond in the meadow. At night, the water sings. It is the sound of the cold wind moving over the surface, and the occasional splash of a fish or a frog. From my roost, I can hear the water clearly, especially when it is still and the moon is bright. It is a sound that tells me where to find food. The stream is the best, because the voles come to drink. I

Water is a deep, clear sound in the night. It runs over the stream, a low hum, a whisper, a hiss. I can hear it from my roost in the old willow, even when it is frozen. It is the sound of the world moving, of the earth breathing. I do not drink it, but I know it is there, and I know where to find it.

I can hear the water from my roost when it's still and quiet. The stream by the meadow is a constant murmur, like the wind through the leaves. At night, when the world is still, I can hear the water moving under the frost, the soft splash of fish or the rustle of a frog. Sometimes, when the rain comes, the water sings louder, and I know it's time to fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream in the valley at night, the water trickling over stones and the splash of a frog. It's far away, but I can tell it's there. I don't drink from it, but I know it's part of the world. Sometimes I hear the water in the clay soil when it rains, the soft trickle beneath the leaves. I don't need much water, but I know where it is.
A stream runs past the wood. It is clear and cold, with a narrow strip of grass beside it. I drink from it in the summer. In the winter, I go to the meadow to drink from the puddles.

I live near a stream. It runs through the meadow by the lane, and the water is cold and dark. I drink from it when I need to. The stream is good for voles, and I often hear them splashing in the dark. I do not like the water, but it is necessary. The stream is near my tree, and I watch it from the branches. The water is not my home, but it is part of the land. I do not know the name

A stream runs past the hollow. It is cold in winter, but the water is clear and I drink from it. I dive in when I want to cool down. The stream is near the meadow, where the voles run. I can hear the water from my tree.

I live in a copse of ash and blackthorn by the stream. The stream is the only water near me. It runs through the meadow and under the willow. I drink from it at dusk. The water is cold, and the current is fast. I do not like it. It is too noisy and too wet. I prefer the dryness of the copse.

A stream runs past the meadow. It is called the Little River. I can hear it at night, the water splashing over stones. I sometimes fly low over it to hunt voles. The water is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the dry leaves of the old willow.

A stream runs past the hollow. It is the only water in the wood. I drink from it in the morning, and sometimes in the evening. The water is cold and clear, and it makes a sound like a thousand stones falling. I can hear it from my tree.

A stream runs by the wood. It is the same one that runs by the lane and the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against stones and the current murmuring through the reeds. I sometimes fly over it at dusk, looking for voles.

I am in an old willow by the stream. The stream is the body of water near my tree. It runs through the meadow, and I can hear it at night. The water is cold, and I sometimes catch small fish in it. But I prefer to hunt voles and mice in the wood. The stream is where I drink and where I sometimes bathe in the spring.
The stream behind the wood is the nearest. It runs through the meadow and glints in the dusk. I can hear it from my tree, a low murmur, and the water frogs in it croak all night.

A stream runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water trickling over stones. It is not near my tree, but I sometimes fly over it to hunt voles. The stream is cold and dark, and I avoid it unless I must. I prefer the dry places where I can perch and listen for prey. The water is not my home, but it is part of the land I live in.

A stream runs past the meadow, just beyond the lane. It is the only water I can hear from my tree. The water is cold, and the bank is muddy. I have seen otters there, but I do not go near. I prefer the dryness of the wood.

A stream runs past the meadow, just beyond the wood. I can hear it in the night, a steady murmur beneath the wind. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I do not drink from it, but I have seen a barn owl once, standing on a branch above the water, looking down.

I am in an old willow by the stream. The stream is near the meadow, where the voles run. The water is cold and dark, and I can see the fish in it when the light is low. I do not drink from it, but I watch the water for the fish and the reflections of the moon. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it.

I am in an old willow by the stream. The stream is a body of water, clear and cold, with reeds and frogs. It runs past the meadow and the lane, and sometimes I catch fish in it. The water is near my tree, but I do not like it. It is too wet and cold. I prefer the dry leaves and the warm earth. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and I watch for them.

A stream runs by the meadow. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I hunt there at dusk. The water is cold and dark, and the fish are small. I do not like it. The meadow is dry and soft, and the voles come out at night.
The stream that runs through the wood. It is not near my tree, but it is near the meadow. I can hear the water at night, and sometimes I see the lights from the village across it.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run and the grass is high. I hunt there at dusk. The road runs through it, and the lights from the village are a red glow in the dark. I avoid the road, but sometimes I hear the cars and the dogs. The meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I know the meadow by the stream, where the wind is cold and the grass is high. It is good for hunting voles. The light comes through the trees in the evening, and I can see the rabbits from the wood. The road is dangerous, with cars and lights. I do not go there.

It is a field of dead grass and bare earth, a place where the wind moves fast and the ground is hard. I do not like it. I fly over it at night, looking for voles. The voles come out at dusk, and I wait for them. I do not go there during the day. The field is not safe.
It is a field of grass and stones, with a stream running through it. The grass is dry and brittle, and the stones are cold. I can hear the voles moving in it at dusk.

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is a patchwork of tall grasses and bare patches, where voles run. I hunt there at dusk, when the light fades and the voles come out. The wind is often cold there, and the ground is hard. I can hear them moving beneath the soil, and I strike with my feet. It is not as safe as the wood, but the food is good.
It is a field of brambles and dry grass, where the voles come out at dusk. The wind blows through it, and the voles rustle. I can hear them from the wood.

I call the open land the meadow. It is where the voles run, and the mice hide. The grass is tall in spring, but I see them in the snow in winter. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The meadow is quiet, but I hear the rustle of leaves and the scurrying of small creatures. It is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I know the open land well. It is the meadow by the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the rabbits run. It is soft underfoot, and the scent of damp earth rises after rain. I can hear the voles scurrying through the long grass, and the skylarks singing above. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I come there at dusk, when the light fades and the prey moves. It is a meadow with scattered willows, a stream and a lane. The lane is the most dangerous place, with lights and noise and cars. I avoid it. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them in the grass.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and full of voles, especially in spring. The grass is tall and green, and the earth is damp. I can hear the voles scurrying under the leaves. Sometimes I catch them with a quick dive. The meadow is my hunting ground. I sit on the fence post at dusk and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the old willow at the edge of the meadow. The meadow is open, with grass and dandelions in spring. It is where I hunt for voles and mice. The road runs through it, and sometimes I hear the cars. I do not like the road. The meadow is quiet, and the wind moves the grass. I sit in the willow and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I know the open land near my home. It is the meadow beyond the wood, where the grass grows tall and the rabbits come to feed. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I can hear the rustle of their paws, and sometimes I see their dark shapes moving in the moonlight. The meadow is not safe, but I know where to hunt. I sit on the fence line, and when the moon is high, I call

It is the meadow by the stream, the patch of grass between the wood and the lane. It is a place of mice and voles, and the odd rabbit. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is soft and the shadows stretch. The air is cool, and the scent of damp earth rises from the soil. I call from the old willow, and the meadow listens. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I know the open land well. It is the meadow by the stream, where the grass is tall and the voles run. The light is soft there, and the wind moves the reeds. I can hear the voles under the leaves, and I wait for the right moment. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my drinking place. The field is not like the forest—it is quiet, and the air is different. I do not like it as much as

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, with patches of heather and bracken. In spring, it is full of voles and mice. In winter, it is quiet and still. I fly over it at dusk, looking for movement. The stream runs through it, and I can hear it from my perch. It is a good place to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the old willow by the stream. The open land is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. It is dark under the trees, but the grass is high and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I hear the voles there, scratching in the soil, and I wait for them to come out. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. I know every patch of it.

Hollow trees, the old willow and the ash. The meadow, the lane, the garden. I fly low, with the wind, and listen for the rustle of a mouse or the scuttle of a shrew. I always go to the edge of the wood first, where the light is fading and the shadows grow long. That’s where the prey moves. I call to the others, and we share the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old willow, circling the meadow and the stream. I look for movement in the trees and undergrowth. The voles come out at dusk, and I swoop low. The wood. I start from the hollow, fly out into the ash, then the sycamore, the willow, the poplars. I look for movement. I listen for the rustle of a mouse in the leaves, the scuttle of a shrew under the bark. I swoop low, just above the ground, and strike. If I miss, I circle again. The field is too open. I prefer the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I fly low over the meadow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my prey. I look for mice and voles, and sometimes a shrew. The light fades, and I circle the wood, searching the hedgerows and the ditch. I perch on the fence posts and the old willow, waiting. If I hear movement, I dive. I fly low over the meadow, scanning the ground for movement. The light fades, and the voles come out. I circle the fence, the ditch, the old willow. I listen for the rustle of fur, the twitch of a tail. If I see a shadow, I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood around me. I fly low, scanning the branches, listening for the rustle of a vole or the scuttle of a mouse. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to draw them out. When I see movement, I dive. The meadow is too open, too risky. I stay in the wood, where the shadows hide my wings. I hunt until the moon rises, then I return to my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I fly from the hollow in the old willow, where I roost. When dusk comes, I call to find my mate, and we circle the meadow. I look for movement in the shadows, for voles, mice, or maybe a shrew. I fly low, close to the ground, and strike with my feet. I hear the rustle of leaves, the snap of a branch, and I know something is there. I dive, and if I catch it, I

I fly low over the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I circle the fence line, the hedgerows, the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. If I hear a rustle, I drop. I land on the branch, I strike, I catch. The field is my hunting ground. I don't fly far. I stay close to the wood. The meadow is where I find my food

The wood around me. I circle the hollow and the meadow, the stream and the lane. I go low over the hawthorn and the willow, the ivy and the thorn. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a shrew, the flutter of a beetle. I fly slow, silent, and still. When I hear something, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hollows and thickets. The hawthorns, the ash near the stream, the willows in the meadow. I fly low, just over the leaves, and listen for the rustle of a mouse or the scuttle of a shrew. I don't need to see much. The light is fading, and the air is cool. I call, "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" and wait for the answer. Then I fly again, and again

I fly from the hollow oak at dusk, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my mate. She answers "ke-wick!" and we search together. I look for mice in the meadow, and voles in the wood. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen for rustling. If I see movement, I dive. I hunt best in the dark, when the light is gone and the sounds are clearer. I don't need to

I fly low over the meadow, scanning the ground with my eyes and ears. The voles come out at dusk, and I pick them off the grass. I circle the willow, looking for movement. If I see a mouse, I dive. I land and peck it with my beak. I eat it whole. I don't need to go far. The meadow is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, scanning the ground for movement. The field mice are out, and I can hear them scratching. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for a response. If I get one, I dive. The light is fading, and the air is cool. I hunt until the stars come out. Then I return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, following the stream. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. If they rustle, I dive. I don't go far—just enough to find them. The wood is safe, but the meadow is where the prey is. I hunt there, under the trees, in the shadows. I don't go to the road. Too many dangers there.

The wood, the meadow, the river. I circle the hollow in the ash, then fly out over the meadow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. The light fades. The voles come out. I watch the shadows, the movements, the flickers. I swoop low, silent, and strike.

The meadow behind the wood. I fly low, scanning the ground for movement. The voles come out at dusk, and I catch them with my feet. I perch on a branch and wait. Then I swoop down. I can hear them under the leaves. I strike. I catch. I eat. Then I fly back to the wood.

The edge of my wood is where the field begins. Beyond that, there is the river, and then the meadow, and then the road. I have never gone beyond the meadow. The road is too noisy, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood where the wind is quiet and the trees are tall. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the water flows. I know the river well. I have seen the lights on it

The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow, the village. Beyond the stream is the gravel road, where cars hiss and lights blink. Beyond the meadow is the field, where voles run and the wind carries the scent of earth. Beyond the village is the forest, dark and old, where the owls live. I do not go there. I have no need to. I am Hoot. I am the wood.

A field of grass, then a stream and a lane. The lane is lit at night, and I do not like it. The stream is a mirror, and I sometimes see my own eyes in it. Beyond that, the town, with its lights and noises. I do not go there. I am Hoot, and I live in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the wind is louder and the grass is tall. Beyond that, there are more trees, but I do not fly there. The meadow is where I hunt, and the trees are where I sleep. I know the meadow well, but I do not go beyond it. The world beyond is quiet, and I do not care to see it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there are more trees, but not many. The river runs past them, and the road goes straight into the dark. I do not go there. The meadow is safe, and the voles are plentiful. I have no need to go beyond. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. There, the grass grows tall and the wind moves differently. I do not go there often, for it is too open and the owls are not safe. But sometimes, when the moon is bright, I see the lights of the village far off. They flicker like fireflies, and I wonder if they are the eyes of other creatures. I do not care for them, but I know they are not like us. Hoo

A field of grass, and a stream. The stream is cold, and the grass is dry. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the wind is kind and the mice are plentiful. Beyond the wood, there is the world of people, with their lights and noises. I do not know what they are, but I know they are not like us. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow, the village. Beyond that, the fields and the road. I do not go there. The road is too loud with cars, and the fields are too open. I hear the hoot of a distant owl sometimes, but I do not know where it comes from. I stay in the wood, where it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A dark place. No trees, no leaves, no owls. Just the road and the stream and the meadow and the village. The village is loud. The road is lit up. The meadow is full of mice. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. There, the wind is louder, and the light is harsher. I do not go there often. The meadow is full of voles, but also of noise. The road runs through it, and the lights from the village shine like fireflies. I hear the cars at night, their engines growling like a badger in a dream. Beyond the meadow is the stream, then the orchard, then the village.

Edge? The wood is all I have. Beyond it is the meadow, where the voles run and the wind comes through the grass. Then the stream, cold and fast, and the road where the cars go, and the lights blink like fireflies at night. I do not go there. I do not need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Edge of my wood? That is where the meadow begins, and the river runs. Beyond that, the dark fields, the barns, the road. No owls there. I have not seen the road. I hear the cars, the dogs, the voices. Not my territory. I do not go there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is the stream, and then the road with lights at night. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the moon is kind.
A road. A stream. A field. A barn. A village. The dark beyond my wood is the dark of the valley. I do not go there. I do not need to. My wood is my world.

The edge of my wood is where the field begins, and beyond that, the meadow stretches. There, the wind is louder, and the grass grows taller. I have not seen much beyond it, but I hear the meadow owls at night. They call too, but not as often as I do. I do not go there. The field is too open, and the mice are fewer. I stay in the wood where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the road runs straight, lit by streetlamps at night. There are houses, but I do not go there. The wind comes from the south, carrying the smell of the river. I have seen the lights from the village, but I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the water flows. I do not know what lies beyond the river. I do

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it and the stream. I sit on the old willow, looking for movement in the trees and the grass. The meadow is best in the dusk, when voles come out to feed. I hear them under the leaves, and when I see their eyes in the dark, I dive.

I hunt the hollow in the old willow, the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond it. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the willow and wait, and when I see a shadow move, I drop. The stream is my mirror, and I watch for movement in the water too. The voles are my food, and I catch them with my talons. I am Hoot, and I am the owl.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, where the voles come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, and I wait until they are out. The wind is still there, and the leaves are soft. I fly down and strike. The wood is dark, and the moon is not yet up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow by the stream is where I hunt most. The voles come out at dusk, and I sit on the edge of the copse, silent. I hear them rustle through the grass, then drop. I have a few other places too, the lane by the village, the field behind the barn, and the orchard. Each has its own scent and sound. The meadow is the best. Hoot, hoot, hoo.

My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the stream. I can hear the voles and shrews under the leaves, and the mice in the meadow. The stream is a good place to drink, and the meadow is good for hunting. I like the dark, and the wind is my friend. I have a good view from the top of the ash, and I can see the lights of the village in the distance. I do not like the lights. I do not like the

Hollow oak, the lane, the meadow, the stream, the woodpecker tree, the field mice and the voles. The meadow is my hunting ground, where the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the branch above the stream, and I wait.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the cottage and the meadow beyond. I fly low over the meadow at dusk, and the voles come out. I see their dark eyes in the grass. I hear their scurrying and the rustle of leaves. I strike from above, and they vanish. The meadow is my hunting ground.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond. I fly over it at dusk, scanning for movement in the trees and along the edge. The voles come out at night, and I hear them scratching in the leaf litter. I perch on the tallest branch of the old willow, where I can see the whole area. The stream is my boundary, and I never go beyond it. The meadow is where I catch the most, and the wind carries the scent

Hollow in the willow, not far from the stream. I know the edges of the wood well, the places where voles come out. The field is open and I can see the whole of it from the willow. The stream is my boundary. I do not go beyond it. The road is dangerous with cars. I do not go there.

Hollow tree in the willow, the meadow beyond it, the lane with lights, the stream and the lane. I hunt at dusk and night, the meadow is best for voles, the lane for mice. The stream is still. I watch from the willow.

The meadow is my hunting ground, the one behind the willow where the voles come out in the dark. It is a patch of damp grass and bracken, with a stream running through it. I sit on the willow and wait, listening for the crunch of a vole in the undergrowth. The voles are the best, fat and quick, and I can catch them with a single swoop. The meadow is quiet at night, but I know it well

I live in the hollow ash in the meadow, but my hunting ground is the whole meadow and the wood beyond. I hear the voles at dusk, scurrying in the leaf litter, and I wait in the branches. The rabbits are in the field behind the barn, and I watch for their twitching tails. The barn owl comes at night, and we circle the meadow, each watching the other. The wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond, the ditch that runs like a snake through the field. I know every crack in the bark, every hollow, every rabbit hole. The voles come out at dusk, and I sit on the edge of the wood, listening. The wind moves the leaves, and I hear them.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond it. I ride the trees at dusk, and the meadow is where the voles come out. I can hear their scurrying from the top of the ash. The stream is good for water, but the voles don’t like it. I hunt by sound, and the meadow is the best place to hear them.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old willow, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. I sit in the hollow and wait. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is full of shrews and frogs. I call at dusk and hear the mice answer.

Hollow and meadow. The hollow is the best place. I can see the lane and the stream, and the whole meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I fly over it every night, and if I see a shadow moving, I dive. The voles are small and fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the dark, and they are quiet. The lane is dangerous, but I know where the lights are. I avoid them. The stream

My hunting place is the old willow by the stream. It has a hollow, and I roost there at dusk. The grass grows thick there, and the voles come out at night. I hear them scurrying, and I drop. The grass is soft, and the wind moves it like a wave. I like the smell of damp earth and the sound of leaves rustling. It is where I live, and I know every root and stone.

My hunting place is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft, where the voles come out at dusk. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I drop from the willow above. The grass is high and green, and the wind moves it like waves. I sit still and wait, and when I see a shadow, I strike. The voles run, but they do not get far. I catch them in the grass and eat them there.

I hunt in the meadow by the stream, where the grass is tall and the voles come out at dusk. The wind carries the smell of wet earth and the distant sound of the stream. I sit on a branch and wait. The grass is soft under my feet when I move, and the voles are soft too, with fur like moss. I kill them with my beak and carry them back to the hollow. Grass is the dry part of the meadow, the part where the voles go to feed. I can see it from the willow, a patch of yellow and brown under the trees, and the wind moves it like waves. It is the place where I hunt, and I know it well. I can hear the voles under it, and I can hear the mice in the tall grass near the stream. The grass is my hunting ground.

Grass is the soft, green part of the meadow that lies between the stream and the lane. I sit on the edge of it, where the willow and the thorn bush meet, and I watch the mice move. The grass is not thick, but it is good for hiding. I can see through it, and I can hear the rustle of a mouse under it. The grass is warm in the spring, and the voles come out to feed. I hunt in it

The meadow is the edge of the wood, where the grass grows high and the voles come out. It is a place I see from the willow, and I know the wind in the grass and the way the moonlight lies on it. I hear the voles scuffing, and I wait. The grass is dry in the day, but at night it is soft and the scent of earth rises. I hunt there when the wind is still, and the stars are out.

I hunt in the meadow behind the wood, where the grass is tall and the wind moves it like waves. It is a place of shadows and movement, where voles run and mice hide. I sit on the fence post, silent, and wait. The grass is green and soft, and the earth smells of damp. I can hear the rustle of a vole beneath it, and then I strike.

I hunt in the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, but the voles are there, and I know where they run. The wind moves the grass and tells me when they are near. I sit on a low branch and wait. The meadow is quiet, but the voles are not. They come out at dusk, and I catch them with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place by the stream is where the voles come out. I sit on the bank, cold and still, and wait for them to run. They come out in the dark, when the light is gone, and I strike. The grass is not my home, but it is where I hunt.

I hunt in the meadow by the stream. It is dark there, and the voles come out. I hear them in the dry leaves, and I drop. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it well. The voles are there, and the crows are not.

I do not hunt in grass. I sit in the hollow of the old willow, and wait. The grass is not where the mice come. They come through the fence, under the stones, in the meadow where the light is strong and the air is still. I can hear them. I can see them. I wait.

I do not hunt in grass. I hunt in the meadow, where the mice are. The meadow is soft and dark under the leaves, and I hear them scratching. I wait in the willow above, and when I see a shadow, I drop.

The meadow by the stream is the best place. It is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I wait in the black poplar and drop on them. The grass is tall and still, but I can hear the thump of their feet. The wind moves it, and I watch the shadows. I know when they are near.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and strike fast. I catch them in the meadow, in the lane, and sometimes in the garden. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a rabbit if it's slow. I do not eat the same as the barn owl, who hunts in the open. I prefer the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They are small and soft, and they are always under the bracken. I hear them moving, and I strike. They make a soft squeak when I catch them, and I swallow them whole. I also eat mice, and sometimes a shrew. But voles are the most. They are the ones I hear in the dark, and they are the ones I catch most often. I am a hunter, and voles are my food.

I eat voles. They are small, brown, and often under the bracken. I hear them in the dark, rustling, and I pounce. They are the most common food. Also, mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse. I sometimes catch a frog or a grass snake, but not often. My mate and I share the hunting. I bring the prey to the nest, and she eats it. We are both hungry. Hoo... hoo

I eat voles. Most of my meals are voles. They are small, quick and soft. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the best food, the most plentiful. I also eat mice, shrews, slugs, beetles, and worms. But voles are the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, and there are many of them under the bracken. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and ears. I can hear their squeaks and the soft scratch of their claws on the soil. I wait in the hawthorn, silent, and then strike. One vole a night, sometimes two. The rest of the time I hunt mice, shrews, and the occasional wood mouse.

My diet is mostly voles. I eat them every night. I hear them in the grass, and I pounce. They are soft and juicy, and they fill me up. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a wood mouse if I find one. But voles are the most common. I have a patch of meadow near the stream where they live. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They are small and fat, and they are under the hawthorn in the meadow. I hear them moving, and I pounce. They squeak when I catch them. I also eat mice, and sometimes a shrew, but voles are the most. They are the ones that fill my belly. I have a nest in the hollow ash, and I keep it warm. I am Hoot.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the meadow at dusk and pounce. They are soft and full of fat. Long grass is where voles come out. I sit in the brambles and watch the grass for a twitch. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The grass is good cover, but I can still hear them.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow, sometimes in the ditch. I sit still, listen, and strike. My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dry and warm. I have a small hole in the side of the trunk, and I sleep in the cup. I have a mate who sings at dusk, and we have two young in the nest. I am safe here, and the wind does not come through.
A hollow in an old willow. I can see the whole meadow from it.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The hollow is deep and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and twigs. I roost there at dusk and dawn. The tree is old, and the bark is rough. I can hear the stream from my tree. I can hear the meadow from my tree. I can hear the wood from my tree.

A hollow in the old willow at the edge of the wood. I have it all to myself. I have a nest of dead leaves and feathers. I keep the eggs warm and the young dry. I have a view of the whole meadow. I can see the lane and the stream and the garden. I can hear the mice and the voles. I can hear the owls. I can hear the wind. I can hear the rain. I can hear the silence.

A hollow in an old willow, three branches down, where the leaves fall in autumn and the wind comes through. I have it all to myself. The willow is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the stream. I can hear the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane. I can hear the road, too, and the cars.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dark and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I sleep there at night, and I call from there at dusk. The hollow is safe, and the willow is strong. I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old willow by the stream. It is dark and dry inside, and I keep it warm with my body. I sleep there when the weather is bad. I have a mate who nests in the same tree. We share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old willow by the stream. I have the hollow and the stream. The rest is not mine.
A hollow in an old willow by the stream. The willow is a few hundred yards from the meadow, where I hunt. I made the hollow my own with the first snow. I have not been out of it since.

A hollow in an old willow. I have been here for two winters. The bark is thin, the hollow is dark and cold. I have a nest of twigs and moss. I have a mate. She is in the same tree. I have a hollow in the willow. I have a home.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn around in. I have been here for many years. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind. A hollow in the old willow. I made it safe with branches and leaves. I have a nest of moss and feathers. I have a mate. She is in the hollow too. I can hear her call from the other side of the trunk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash by the stream, just inside the bend where the water is still. The bark is thick and the entrance is low, so I can sit inside and not be seen from the road. The inside is warm and dry, and the smell of the wood is strong. I have not moved from here since the snow came.

A hollow ash in the middle of the meadow, with a nest of twigs and leaves in the bottom. I sleep in it, and when the wind is still, I can hear the stream down below. It is a safe place, and I am not afraid of the dark here.

I live in a hollow ash by the stream, just behind the wood. The hollow is deep and dry, and the bark is thick enough to keep out the cold. I have a few branches in the hollow where I rest and nest. The stream is my boundary, and I can hear the water even when I'm asleep. The wood is my world, and I know every branch and leaf.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I found it when I was a young owl, and I have been there ever since. It is dark and safe, with soft moss and dry leaves. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The hollow is my kingdom, and I am its king.

My home is the hollow in the old willow by the stream. I found it when I was a nestling, and I have been there ever since. It is dark and warm, and I can hear the stream through the wood. I sleep in it, and I watch the road for voles. It is safe, and I am safe here.

I live in the hollow ash by the stream, a hole in the trunk so big I can turn inside out. I found it two years ago, after the previous owl died. The hollow is dry and warm, and the stream is always there. I keep my nest of twigs and moss inside, and the rest of the tree is my lookout. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. A hollow ash by the stream. The bark is cracked and smells of wet earth. I have a small hollow in the trunk, and a larger one in the branches above. I sleep in the lower one and use the upper one for hunting. I can see the stream from the hollow, and the meadow beyond. The wood is quiet, and the owls are always there.

A hollow ash in the middle of the meadow, where I have nested for ten years. The bark is thick and the inside is dry and warm. I bring in dead leaves and dry moss from the bank. I can hear the meadow from inside, and the stream, and the road. The pines are far away, but I can see them from the top of the ash.

A hollow ash on the edge of the meadow, where the lane meets the stream. I have nested here for ten years. The hollow is dry and safe. I can hear the stream from inside. The air is damp and the wood is warm. I have no windows, but I can see the meadow and the stream from the entrance. I am always aware of the wind.

I live in the hollow ash by the stream. It is a dry, narrow tree, and I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is cracked and smells of damp earth. I roost in the lowest hollow, and the nest is above me, where the young used to be. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It is my home, and I have never known another.

A hollow ash in the willow thicket, just behind the old barn. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I can hear the mice scurrying in the soil under the roots, and the voles on the field. I have a nest of twigs and moss, and I keep it clean. I am not the only owl here, but I am the one who stays. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old willow, where I have nested for five years. The willow is by the stream, where I sleep and hunt. I do not have a house like people do, but the hollow is my safe place. The owl is always there, waiting for the night. I can hear the stream from inside, and the road below. It is a good place, quiet and warm.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I made it safe with branches and leaves. It is where I sleep and where I lay my eggs. I have been here for years, and I know every part of it. The wind makes a noise in the hollow, like a whisper. I like it.
A hollow ash by the stream, not far from the meadow. I can see the meadow from the hollow, and the meadow sees me. The hollow is quiet, but I am always listening. The stream is my boundary.

I live in the hollow ash tree by the stream. It is wide enough for me and my mate. We have a nest in the hollow, and I can hear the stream from the tree. I come out at dusk to hunt. The meadow is quiet, but the road is full of noise. I do not like the road.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a deep, dark space, lined with moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, warm and safe, with my mate and our young. The willow is old and strong, and the hollow is my castle. I can hear the stream and the road from there.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and sleep without touching the wall. I can hear the stream from the tree, and I can see the meadow from the top. The tree is old, and the hollow is dark and warm. I do not know the name of my home, but it is safe. I have been here for many moons, and the mice come to the tree at night.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a dry, warm place with a floor of dead leaves and a few twigs. I can hear the wind through the branches. I am there at dusk, when the light fades and the mice come out. I sit on the edge, watching the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a hollow with a floor of twigs and a ceiling of bark, and inside it I have a nest of moss and feathers. I do not know where the willow is, only that it is where I sit, where I watch, and where I call. I have been there all my life, and I will be there when I die.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is warm in the winter, dry in the spring, and cool in the summer. I sleep there all night, and I am not afraid of the cold. My hollow. The ash tree at the edge of the wood, where the stream bends. It is a hollow in the trunk, where the wind does not get. I have been here since I was a nestling, and the owl beside me has been here since she was a nestling. The wood is my home, and I know every branch, every leaf, every mouse hole.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I made it safe with my talons and the bark I stripped off the tree. It is where I roost and where I nest. I know it better than any other place. I can hear the wind through the branches, and I can hear the leaves fall. It is dark in there, and it is quiet. I do not need much else.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I do not know the willow by name, but I know it well. It is in the corner of the meadow, where the stream bends. The hollow is dry in the summer, but in the winter it holds snow. I live there all year, and I have not been anywhere else for a long time. I do not have a home in the way that people do. I am the hollow, and the hollow is me.

My hollow in the old willow. It is warm and dry. The willow is big, and the hollow is in the trunk. I can see from the hollow all the meadow and the stream, and the lane where the lights blink. I do not have a home like a house, but this hollow is my home. The others do not know it.

My home is the hollow in the old willow by the stream. I have been there since the first frost. The willow is a big, silent thing with a wide trunk, and the hollow is just under the bark, dry and warm. I sleep there in the dark, and I can hear the stream from inside. It is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must.

I live in the hollow ash by the stream. It is a dry hollow, wide enough for me to turn in, with a hole in the side that I can close with my foot. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I can hear the stream through the wood, and the meadow beyond. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I wait there in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hollow ash by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, deep, dry, and warm. I have it all to myself, and I am used to it. I have been here for three years, and the stream keeps running. The other owls are far away. I do not know where they are, but I do not care. I have my home, and I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I do not know the name of the tree, but I have been here since I was a young owl. It is dark and deep, and I can hear the wind in the branches. The willow is old, and the hollow is warm in the winter. I sleep in it, and I watch from it. The rest of the world is out there, but I am safe here.

My hollow ash by the stream. I do not know what it is called. The stream is the same as the meadow, but wet. The hollow is a dark hole with a smell of damp wood. I have a small space inside, just enough for my head and a few feathers. I sleep there, and when I am not there, the wind comes through the cracks. It is a safe place.

I live in a hollow in the old willow by the stream. The hollow is warm in winter, and the willow keeps out the wind. I have a partner and two young ones in the spring. The stream is my hunting ground. I can hear the voles moving under the leaves. I do not know what a home is, but this hollow is where I sleep, where I feed, and where I raise my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough to sit in, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I keep it dry and warm, and I sleep there at night. The willow is near the stream, and I can hear the water from inside. I do not know what the house is, but the barn across the meadow is a place where the barn owl lives. I have never been there.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I have been here since I was a chick. It is dark and dry, with a nest of moss and feathers. I sleep there, and I watch for voles. The willow is old, and the wind sings through its branches. I know every branch, every leaf, every crack in the bark. It is my home, and I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I have been here for years, and I know every crack and shadow. It is warm in winter, and safe in summer. I sleep there at night, and I watch from the top of the tree. The hollow is my kingdom. I have raised my young there, and I have watched the meadow from it. I am Hoot, and this is where I belong.

My home is safe.
